messages.subject_clean: Online course: Statistical Ideas and Controversies
messages.body_plain:
Hello R-SIG-ECOLOGY members

A reminder - Ecological analyses can serve different purposes, from exploring observations to making predictions. Seminal Ideas & Controversies in Statistics: A Short Course is a 2-day seminar livestreaming November 3?4 with Roderick Little (Department of Biostatistics, University of Michigan). Parametric modelling and algorithmic prediction raise different questions about the aims of data analysis. Researchers analysing ecological data in R can use the discussion to consider whether their methods match their scientific questions. The course also covers exploratory data analysis and computer-intensive methods, including the bootstrap.

Details and registration: https://instats.org/seminar/seminal-ideas-and-controversies-in-stati-2
Further information is available on the seminar page.


Best wishes

Michael Zyphur
Director and Co-founder
Instats | instats.org

messages.subject: [R-sig-eco] Genomics and Bioinformatics for Non-Model Organisms (BNMO01) – Applications for Ecological Research
messages.subject_clean: Genomics and Bioinformatics for Non-Model Organisms (BNMO01) – Applications for Ecological Research
messages.body_plain:
Genomics and Bioinformatics for Non-Model Organisms (BNMO01) ? Applications for Ecological Research

7?11 December 2026 | 25 hours | ?400 | Live Online

Course information and registration<https://prstats.org/course/genomics-and-bioinformatics-for-non-model-organisms-bnmo01/>

Delivered by Dr Nikolay Oskolkov, a bioinformatician and computational biologist specialising in genomics, population genetics, bioinformatics and computational biology.

The increasing availability of high-throughput sequencing data is transforming ecological research, providing new opportunities to investigate genetic diversity, population structure, adaptive variation, gene expression and the genomic basis of ecological traits.

However, analysing genomic data from non-model organisms presents substantial challenges, particularly when reference genomes and established genomic resources are limited.

Genomics and Bioinformatics for Non-Model Organisms (BNMO01) provides practical training in computational approaches for analysing genomic and transcriptomic datasets, with a focus on variant discovery, RNA-seq analysis, differential gene expression, population structure and the integration of multiple types of genomic information.

For researchers working in molecular ecology, conservation genomics, evolutionary ecology and population genetics, these methods provide valuable tools for investigating genetic variation in natural populations and exploring the molecular mechanisms associated with ecological and evolutionary processes.

The course combines theoretical instruction with practical bioinformatics exercises, introducing computational workflows and statistical approaches for analysing complex genomic datasets.

What you'll gain

  *   Understand the challenges of genomic analysis in non-model organisms

  *   Explore genomic and transcriptomic data processing workflows

  *   Perform quality control and preprocessing of sequencing data

  *   Understand sequence alignment and variant discovery

  *   Apply GATK workflows for identifying and processing genetic variants

  *   Explore genomic variation within and among populations

  *   Understand the use of Principal Component Analysis (PCA) for investigating population structure

  *   Apply UMAP for dimensionality reduction and visualisation of genomic data

  *   Understand RNA-seq analysis workflows

  *   Explore RNA-seq read alignment using STAR

  *   Quantify gene expression using featureCounts

  *   Understand statistical approaches to differential gene expression

  *   Explore relationships between genetic variation and gene expression through expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) analysis

  *   Understand approaches to integrating genomic and transcriptomic datasets

  *   Explore the role of machine learning in genomic data analysis

  *   Develop a foundation for reproducible computational analysis of genomic datasets

Applications for ecological research

The methods introduced in BNMO01 are relevant to ecological questions involving:

  *   Conservation genomics: investigating genetic variation in threatened or poorly studied species

  *   Population genetics: exploring genetic differentiation and population structure in natural populations

  *   Evolutionary ecology: examining genomic variation associated with ecological and phenotypic differences

  *   Environmental adaptation: investigating candidate genes and genomic regions potentially associated with environmental responses

  *   Ecological transcriptomics: analysing gene expression differences between populations, treatments or environmental conditions

  *   Molecular ecology: integrating genetic and transcriptomic information with ecological research

  *   Wildlife and plant genomics: applying bioinformatics workflows to species with limited genomic resources

  *   Genotype?phenotype relationships: investigating associations between genetic variation, gene expression and complex biological traits

Course format

  *   Dates: 7?11 December 2026

  *   Duration: 5 days, 5 hours per day ? 25 hours total

  *   Format: Live online

  *   Instructor: Dr Nikolay Oskolkov

  *   Combination of theoretical lectures and practical computational exercises

  *   Training in genomic and transcriptomic analysis workflows

  *   Course fee: ?400

Who is this course for?

This course will be particularly relevant to researchers and postgraduate students working in:

  *   Molecular ecology

  *   Ecological genomics

  *   Conservation genetics and genomics

  *   Evolutionary ecology

  *   Population genetics and genomics

  *   Environmental genomics

  *   Quantitative and statistical genomics

  *   Wildlife and plant genomics

  *   Transcriptomics and gene expression

  *   Bioinformatics and computational biology

Researchers who already use R for ecological data analysis and wish to expand into genomic and transcriptomic methods may find the course particularly valuable.

Although BNMO01 uses specialist bioinformatics software rather than focusing exclusively on R, its analytical concepts?including multivariate analysis, dimensionality reduction, differential expression and statistical modelling?are relevant to researchers interested in extending their quantitative ecological workflows to genomic data.

Why take this course?

Ecological research increasingly involves integrating genomic and transcriptomic information with environmental, phenotypic and population-level data.

For example, researchers investigating environmental adaptation may wish to understand how genetic variation differs among populations, while those studying physiological responses to environmental stress may be interested in changes in gene expression.

Similarly, conservation genomic studies often require the identification and interpretation of genetic variants, assessment of population structure and comparison of genomic variation across populations.

These analyses involve substantial computational and statistical challenges, particularly when working with organisms that lack comprehensive reference genomic resources.

BNMO01 introduces practical methods for addressing these challenges, covering workflows for variant discovery, RNA-seq analysis, gene expression quantification and the integration of genomic information.

The course also introduces dimensionality reduction techniques such as PCA and UMAP, which are useful for exploring high-dimensional genomic datasets and identifying patterns of genetic variation.

For ecologists already familiar with multivariate analysis and statistical modelling in R, these methods provide a natural extension into ecological and evolutionary genomics.

The course also explores eQTL analysis and multi-omics integration, providing a foundation for investigating relationships between genetic variation and gene expression.

Although the practical exercises are focused on genomic and bioinformatics workflows rather than conventional ecological datasets, the methods are directly applicable to research involving natural populations, non-model species, environmental responses and evolutionary processes.

By the end of the course, participants will have developed a stronger understanding of how to process, analyse and interpret genomic and transcriptomic datasets, helping them incorporate these approaches into their own ecological research.

Please feel free to share this course with colleagues, friends, research groups, labs, and others within your institute, organisation, or wider ecological research network.

Learn more & enrol

View the full course and register<https://prstats.org/course/genomics-and-bioinformatics-for-non-model-organisms-bnmo01/>

Best wishes,

Oliver Hooker

messages.subject: [R-sig-eco] Interactive Maps with tmap and Shiny (IMTS02) – Applications for Ecology + Additional Recorded GIS & Mapping Courses
messages.subject_clean: Interactive Maps with tmap and Shiny (IMTS02) – Applications for Ecology + Additional Recorded GIS & Mapping Courses
messages.body_plain:
Interactive Maps with tmap and Shiny (IMTS02) ? Applications for Ecology + Additional Recorded GIS & Mapping Courses

9?11 December 2026 | 15 hours | ?350 | Live Online

Course information and registration<https://prstats.org/course/interactive-maps-with-tmap-and-shiny-imts02/>

Delivered by Dr Martijn Tennekes, principal author of the widely used tmap R package, this practical three-day course introduces the tools and techniques needed to create, customise and publish interactive maps and web-based spatial visualisations using R.

For ecologists, interactive mapping provides powerful ways to explore and communicate species distributions, habitat characteristics, biodiversity patterns, ecological survey data and environmental change.

Using tmap, Leaflet, Mapbox, MapLibre GL and Shiny, participants will learn how to transform geographic datasets into interactive maps and applications suitable for research, conservation planning and environmental communication.

What you'll learn

  *   Create interactive maps using tmap in R

  *   Customise map layouts, legends, colours and geographic layers

  *   Add interactive features including tooltips, pop-ups and layer controls

  *   Explore modern web mapping with Leaflet, Mapbox and MapLibre GL

  *   Use tmap.mapgl for high-performance interactive mapping

  *   Develop interactive spatial visualisations and dashboards using Shiny

  *   Export and publish interactive maps for sharing online

  *   Build reproducible workflows for spatial data visualisation

Applications for ecological research

The methods are particularly relevant to:

  *   Species distributions: interactive mapping of occurrence records and geographic ranges

  *   Biodiversity monitoring: visualising species richness, survey observations and ecological patterns

  *   Habitat and landscape ecology: exploring land-cover, habitat boundaries and environmental gradients

  *   Conservation planning: communicating protected areas, management zones and conservation priorities

  *   Marine and freshwater ecology: mapping aquatic habitats, monitoring stations and species observations

  *   Environmental monitoring: presenting spatial environmental data through interactive maps and dashboards

Although the course uses general spatial datasets, the methods are directly transferable to ecological and conservation research.

Course format

  *   Dates: 9?11 December 2026

  *   Time: 15:00?20:00 GMT each day

  *   Duration: 15 hours

  *   Format: Live online via Zoom

  *   Instructor: Dr Martijn Tennekes

  *   Hands-on practical exercises using R, tmap and Shiny

  *   Recordings available for 30 days

  *   Course materials and code provided

  *   Fee: ?350

Who should attend?

Researchers, postgraduate students and professionals working in ecology, conservation biology, environmental science, spatial ecology, biodiversity monitoring, GIS and ecological data visualisation.

Participants should have basic familiarity with R. Previous experience with Shiny or interactive web mapping is not required.

Additional recorded courses ? GIS, spatial analysis and mapping

PR Stats also offers the following recorded courses, allowing researchers to develop their spatial analysis and mapping skills at their own pace.

1. A FREE Introduction to Spatial Data Visualisation and Mapping in R (FMAPPR)

A free introduction to mapping with tmap in R, delivered by the package author.

View FREE course<https://prstats.org/course/free-course-introduction-to-spatial-data-visualisation-and-mapping-in-r-fmappr/>

2. Interactive Maps with tmap and Shiny (IMTSPR)

The recorded alternative to IMTS02, covering static and interactive maps, customised layouts and publishing spatial visualisations.

View recorded course<https://prstats.org/course/interactive-maps-with-tmap-and-shiny-imtspr/>

3. Introduction to QGIS and Spatial Data Analysis Workflows (IQGIPR)

Learn essential QGIS skills, including spatial data processing, geographic mapping and GIS workflows.

View recorded course<https://prstats.org/course/introduction-to-qgis-and-spatial-data-analysis-workflows-iqgipr/>

4. Spatial Data Visualisation and Mapping using tmap (TMAPPR)

A comprehensive 20-hour recorded course covering static and interactive mapping using tmap, sf, terra and stars.

View recorded course<https://prstats.org/course/spatial-data-visualisation-and-mapping-using-tmap-tmappr/>

5. Adapting to the Recent Changes in R Spatial Packages (PROJPR)

Update your R spatial skills, transitioning from sp/raster to sf/terra/PROJ7.

View recorded course<https://prstats.org/course/adapting-to-the-recent-changes-in-r-spatial-packages-sf-terra-proj-library-projpr/>

6. Advanced Static Cartography (ASCRPR)

Learn to produce clear, publication-quality maps using advanced cartographic techniques in R.

View recorded course<https://prstats.org/course/advanced-static-cartography-ascrpr/>

Please feel free to share these courses with colleagues, friends, research groups, labs, and others within your institute, organisation, or wider ecological research network.

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,
Ancient Microbiome and Pathogen Genomics (AMPG01) ? Applications for Ecology

11?15 January 2027 | 25 hours | ?400 | Live Online

Course information and registration<https://prstats.org/course/ancient-microbiome-and-pathogen-genomics-ampg01/>

Delivered by Dr Nikolay Oskolkov, a bioinformatician and computational biologist specialising in genomics, bioinformatics and computational biology.

Ancient DNA and metagenomic sequencing provide exciting opportunities to investigate past microbial communities, host?microbe relationships, pathogen evolution and changes in microbial biodiversity through time.

Ancient Microbiome and Pathogen Genomics (AMPG01) introduces practical bioinformatics methods for identifying, authenticating and analysing microbial and pathogen DNA recovered from ancient biological and environmental samples.

For ecologists, these approaches offer valuable insights into historical microbial diversity, ecological community change, ancient host-associated microbiomes and the long-term dynamics of pathogens and microbial populations.

This five-day course combines theoretical instruction with practical computational exercises, covering the challenges of ancient DNA analysis and the specialist workflows required to investigate ancient microbial and pathogen genomes.

What you'll learn

  *   Understand the principles and challenges of ancient microbial DNA analysis

  *   Explore ancient microbiome and pathogen metagenomic datasets

  *   Perform sequencing quality control and preprocessing using fastp and cutadapt

  *   Identify and remove host-derived sequencing reads

  *   Conduct taxonomic classification using Kraken and sourmash

  *   Work with microbial reference databases

  *   Authenticate ancient DNA using mapDamage and PMDtools

  *   Identify potential contamination and evaluate the reliability of microbial assignments

  *   Explore contamination assessment tools including decontam, Recentrifuge and GENEX

  *   Understand specialised ancient metagenomic workflows using aMeta

  *   Explore microbial genome assembly and downstream genomic analysis

  *   Investigate patterns of microbial diversity and community composition

  *   Use PCA and UMAP to explore high-dimensional genomic datasets

  *   Interpret ancient microbial and pathogen genomic results

Applications for ecological research

The methods introduced in AMPG01 are relevant to:

  *   Microbial ecology: investigating the composition and diversity of ancient microbial communities

  *   Palaeoecology: reconstructing aspects of historical microbial biodiversity and ecological change

  *   Host?microbiome ecology: exploring ancient microbial communities associated with animals and other organisms

  *   Disease ecology: investigating historical pathogens and their relationships with host populations

  *   Evolutionary ecology: examining microbial and pathogen genomic variation through time

  *   Environmental microbiology: analysing microbial DNA recovered from ancient environmental material

  *   Community ecology: comparing microbial assemblages across historical samples and environmental contexts

  *   Conservation and biodiversity research: providing historical perspectives on microbial diversity and ecological change

Course format

  *   Dates: 11?15 January 2027

  *   Duration: 5 days, 5 hours per day ? 25 hours total

  *   Format: Live online

  *   Instructor: Dr Nikolay Oskolkov

  *   Combination of lectures and hands-on computational exercises

  *   Practical training in ancient DNA and metagenomic bioinformatics

  *   Course fee: ?400

Who should attend?

Researchers, postgraduate students and professionals working in microbial ecology, palaeoecology, environmental microbiology, molecular ecology, disease ecology, evolutionary biology, ancient DNA research, metagenomics and bioinformatics.

The course is particularly relevant to researchers interested in using ancient microbial DNA to investigate historical ecological communities, host-associated microbiomes and pathogen evolution.

Why take this course?

Microbial communities play fundamental roles in ecological systems, influencing nutrient cycling, host health, disease dynamics and ecosystem functioning. However, most microbial ecological research focuses on contemporary samples.

Ancient DNA provides an opportunity to extend these investigations into the past, allowing researchers to explore microbial communities and pathogen diversity across historical and archaeological timescales.

Ancient metagenomics can provide valuable evidence of how microbial assemblages, host-associated communities and pathogen populations have changed through time.

Analysing ancient microbial DNA presents particular challenges, including DNA fragmentation, post-mortem damage, contamination and difficulties distinguishing authentic ancient sequences from modern microbial material.

AMPG01 introduces practical computational approaches for addressing these challenges, combining sequencing quality control, taxonomic identification, ancient DNA authentication and downstream genomic analysis.

For ecologists interested in historical biodiversity, microbial community change or disease ecology, these methods provide a foundation for incorporating ancient genomic evidence into ecological and evolutionary research.

Although the course is focused on ancient microbiome and pathogen genomics rather than conventional ecological survey data, its methods are particularly relevant to microbial ecology, palaeoecology, host?microbiome research and the historical ecology of infectious diseases.

Learn more & enrol

View the full course and register<https://prstats.org/course/ancient-microbiome-and-pathogen-genomics-ampg01/>

Please feel free to share this course with colleagues, friends, research groups, labs, and others within your institute, organisation, or wider ecological research network.

Questions?

Best wishes,

Oliver Hooker

Ancient DNA provides opportunities to investigate historical biodiversity, population dynamics, species evolution, migration and past ecosystems.

For ecologists and evolutionary biologists, ancient genomic data offer valuable insights into historical genetic diversity, population structure, ancestry, gene flow and evolutionary change.

This course introduces practical bioinformatics methods for processing, authenticating and analysing ancient DNA, from raw sequencing data through to population genetic analysis.

Applications for ecological research

The methods introduced in ADNA01 are particularly relevant to:

  *   Evolutionary ecology: investigating historical population structure, genetic variation and evolutionary change

  *   Palaeoecology: exploring ancient biological communities and historical biodiversity

  *   Conservation genetics: providing historical context for contemporary genetic diversity and population differentiation

  *   Population ecology: investigating past population dynamics, migration and demographic history

  *   Molecular ecology: analysing ancient genomic data to investigate ancestry, admixture and gene flow

Why take this course?

Understanding how populations and ecosystems have changed through time is central to many areas of ecological and evolutionary research.

Ancient DNA provides direct genetic evidence from historical populations, helping researchers investigate evolutionary and demographic processes that cannot always be reconstructed from contemporary samples alone.

However, ancient genomic data present particular analytical challenges, including DNA degradation, contamination, low sequencing coverage and post-mortem damage.

ADNA01 provides practical training in the specialist computational workflows needed to address these challenges, combining ancient DNA authentication, sequence processing and population genetic analysis.

Participants will develop skills applicable to investigations of historical biodiversity, population structure, genetic diversity, ancestry, migration and evolutionary change.

18?22 January 2027 | 35 hours | ?490 | Live Online

PR Stats is pleased to announce Spatial and Spatio-Temporal Modelling Using R-INLA (SSTM03), a practical five-day online course delivered by Dr Virgilio G?mez-Rubio, a leading specialist in Bayesian inference, spatial statistics and statistical computing, and author of Bayesian Inference with INLA.

Spatial and temporal dependencies are fundamental features of ecological data. Species observations, environmental measurements, habitat characteristics and biodiversity patterns frequently exhibit spatial autocorrelation and change over time, presenting challenges for conventional statistical approaches.

This course introduces Bayesian spatial and spatio-temporal modelling using Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA), providing practical training in fitting, interpreting and visualising complex spatial models in R.

For ecologists, these methods offer powerful approaches for investigating species distributions, ecological variation, environmental processes, spatial dependence and changes in ecological patterns through time.

What you'll learn

  *   Understand the principles of Bayesian inference using INLA

  *   Fit and interpret Bayesian models using the R-INLA package

  *   Extend generalised linear mixed models (GLMMs) using INLA

  *   Work with different types of spatial and spatio-temporal data in R

  *   Visualise spatial datasets and produce maps of model results

  *   Fit spatial models for lattice (areal) data, including observations aggregated by geographic regions

  *   Model continuous spatial data, such as environmental measurements and ecological variables

  *   Analyse spatial point-pattern data

  *   Develop spatio-temporal models for lattice, continuous and point-pattern datasets

  *   Interpret model outputs, spatial effects and associated uncertainty

  *   Apply Bayesian spatial modelling techniques to research datasets

Applications for ecological research

The methods introduced in SSTM03 are particularly relevant to:

  *   Species distributions: modelling geographic variation in species occurrence and abundance

  *   Spatial ecology: accounting for spatial autocorrelation and geographic dependence in ecological observations

  *   Biodiversity monitoring: investigating spatial and temporal variation in biodiversity patterns

  *   Habitat ecology: modelling relationships between ecological responses and spatially structured environmental variables

  *   Conservation biology: identifying geographic patterns and changes relevant to conservation planning

  *   Marine and freshwater ecology: analysing spatially referenced observations and environmental monitoring data

  *   Environmental science: modelling spatial variation in pollution, climate-related variables and environmental processes

  *   Long-term ecological monitoring: investigating changes in ecological patterns across space and time

Course format

  *   Dates: 18?22 January 2027

  *   Time: 14:00?21:00 GMT daily

  *   Duration: 5 days, 35 hours total

  *   Format: Live online via Zoom

  *   Instructor: Dr Virgilio G?mez-Rubio

  *   Fee: ?490

  *   Lectures and hands-on practical exercises using R-INLA

  *   Course materials, code and datasets provided

  *   Opportunities to discuss participants' own research data

  *   Recordings available for 30 days, allowing participants in different time zones to follow the course

  *   Post-course email support for 30 days

Who should attend?

Researchers, postgraduate students and professionals working in ecology, spatial ecology, conservation biology, environmental science, biodiversity monitoring, marine ecology, freshwater ecology, biogeography and ecological statistics.

The course is designed for intermediate to advanced R users with a foundational understanding of statistics and Bayesian inference. Familiarity with generalised linear models and mixed models is beneficial, although previous experience with spatial or spatio-temporal modelling is not required.

Why take this course?

Ecological datasets are rarely independent across space and time. Nearby sampling locations may share similar environmental conditions, species observations may be spatially clustered, and ecological processes frequently change over time.

Ignoring these dependencies can affect statistical inference, uncertainty estimates and ecological predictions.

R-INLA provides an efficient Bayesian framework for modelling spatial and spatio-temporal dependence, allowing researchers to fit complex hierarchical models without relying exclusively on computationally intensive Markov chain Monte Carlo methods.

SSTM03 combines an introduction to INLA with practical modelling of lattice, continuous and point-pattern data, progressing from spatial models to their spatio-temporal extensions.

By the end of the course, participants will have developed practical skills for fitting, interpreting and visualising Bayesian spatial and spatio-temporal models, with applications across ecological and environmental research.

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

Animal Movement Ecology – From Traditional Statistical Methods to Deep Learning

Live and recorded courses | R & Python | Movement Analysis, Habitat Selection and Spatial Modelling

PR Stats is pleased to announce a series of practical courses covering animal movement ecology, GPS tracking data, home range estimation, resource and step selection, deep learning and spatial modelling.

These courses provide complementary approaches to analysing animal movement, from established statistical methods in R to advanced movement prediction using deep learning in Python.

1. Movement Ecology (the Analysis of Movement Data) (MOVE10)

10–14 May 2027 | 40 hours | £480 | Live Online

https://prstats.org/course/movement-ecology-the-analysis-of-movement-data-move10/

Instructors: Prof. Luca Börger and Prof. Garrett M. Street

This comprehensive five-day course introduces the concepts, statistical methods and computational tools used to analyse animal movement data across ecological systems.

Combining theoretical instruction with practical exercises in R, participants will explore movement patterns, habitat selection, spatial behaviour and animal interactions.

Topics include:

  *   Movement path analysis, step lengths, turning angles and movement classification

  *   Home range estimation, utilisation distributions and kernel density methods

  *   Spatial and temporal interactions between individuals

  *   First-passage time and residence time analysis

  *   Resource selection functions (RSFs) and habitat selection

  *   Step-selection functions (SSFs), including movement-integrated approaches

  *   Simulation of utilisation and occurrence distributions

Applications: Wildlife tracking, migration, dispersal, foraging behaviour, habitat use, conservation planning and animal movement research.

2. Deep Learning for Animal Movement with deepSSF (DSSF01)

15–18 February 2027 | 16 hours | £325 | Live Online

https://prstats.org/course/deep-learning-for-animal-movement-with-deepssf-dssf01/

Instructor: Dr. Scott Forrester

This four-day course introduces deep learning approaches to animal movement modelling, using the deepSSF framework and Python.

Building on the principles of step-selection functions, deepSSF uses neural networks to model complex relationships between movement behaviour, habitat characteristics and environmental conditions.

Topics include:

  *   Introduction to predictive movement modelling and deepSSF

  *   Neural networks, convolutional layers and mixture density networks

  *   Preparing GPS tracking and environmental raster datasets

  *   Building and training models using Python and PyTorch

  *   Evaluating predictive performance using withheld data

  *   Simulating animal movement trajectories

  *   Predicting space use and landscape connectivity

Applications: GPS telemetry, movement prediction, habitat selection, landscape connectivity, ecological forecasting and conservation planning.

This course is particularly relevant to researchers looking to extend traditional step-selection approaches using modern machine learning methods.

3. Movement Ecology (the Analysis of Movement Data) (MOVEPR)

40 hours | £480 | Recorded – Study at Your Own Pace

https://prstats.org/course/movement-ecology-the-analysis-of-movement-data-movepr/

For researchers unable to attend MOVE10 live, PR Stats also offers a recorded version of Movement Ecology, covering the same core analytical framework and methods.

The course includes:

  *   Movement path analysis and classification

  *   Home range estimation and spatial interactions

  *   Resource and habitat selection

  *   Step-selection functions

  *   Practical movement modelling exercises in R

Participants receive access to recorded lectures, practical exercises, code and datasets, allowing them to work through the material at their own pace.

Complementary course – Bayesian spatial and spatio-temporal modelling
4. Spatial and Spatio-Temporal Modelling Using R-INLA (SSTM03)

18–22 January 2027 | 35 hours | £490 | Live Online

https://prstats.org/course/spatial-and-spatio-temporal-modelling-using-r-inla-sstm03/

Instructor: Dr Virgilio Gómez-Rubio

For researchers interested in extending their spatial modelling skills, SSTM03 introduces Bayesian spatial and spatio-temporal modelling using R-INLA.

The course covers:

  *   Bayesian inference using Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA)

  *   Spatial models for areal, continuous and point-pattern data

  *   Spatial and temporal dependence

  *   Hierarchical Bayesian modelling

  *   Spatio-temporal model development

  *   Spatial prediction, visualisation and uncertainty

Although not specifically focused on animal movement, these methods complement movement ecology research by providing tools for analysing spatially structured ecological observations, habitat variation and environmental processes through time.

Who should attend?

These courses are relevant to researchers, postgraduate students and professionals working in movement ecology, behavioural ecology, wildlife biology, conservation biology, spatial ecology, marine ecology, ornithology, habitat selection, ecological modelling and environmental science.

Together, the courses provide opportunities to develop expertise across three complementary areas:

Movement analysis in R → Deep learning and movement prediction in Python → Bayesian spatial and spatio-temporal modelling

Participants can select individual courses according to their research interests and experience.

Live courses include practical exercises, course materials, access to session recordings for 30 days and post-course email support.

Please feel free to share these courses with colleagues, friends, research groups, labs and others within your institute, organisation or wider ecological research network.

For further information or questions, please contact oliver at prstats.org<mailto:oliver at prstats.org>.

Best wishes,

Oliver Hooker
PR Stats
